title: Attacker impersonates the user with stolen credentials
description: Credentials obtained through phishing, credential stuffing or reuse let an attacker act as this actor.
mitigation: Require multi-factor authentication, detect anomalous sign-ins, rate-limit and lock out repeated failures.

title: Rogue system pretends to be this external system
description: Without strong service authentication, any system able to reach the interface can claim to be this actor.
mitigation: Authenticate the system with mutual TLS, signed tokens or managed identities instead of shared secrets or IP allow-lists.

title: Automated agent is hijacked or acts on injected instructions
description: An automated or AI agent can be steered by crafted input (e.g. prompt injection) to act with its own identity on an attacker's behalf.
mitigation: Give the agent least-privilege, scoped credentials; require human confirmation for sensitive actions; treat all agent input as untrusted.

title: Identity provider is compromised or misconfigured
description: If this actor provides authentication for others, a weakness in it lets attackers mint valid identities.
mitigation: Harden and monitor the identity provider, validate token issuer, audience and signature, rotate signing keys.

title: Actor denies having performed an action
description: Without reliable attribution the actor can plausibly deny initiating a transaction or change.
mitigation: Log security-relevant actions with authenticated identity, timestamp and request id to tamper-evident storage; use signed receipts for high-value actions.

title: Caller bypasses authentication
description: Endpoints or message handlers that do not consistently authenticate callers can be invoked anonymously.
mitigation: Authenticate every entry point by default (deny unless explicitly public); test for unauthenticated access.

title: Session token is stolen or fixated
description: Session cookies or bearer tokens leaked through XSS, logs or insecure transport let attackers reuse a victim's session.
mitigation: Use HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies; short-lived tokens with rotation; bind sessions to the client where feasible.

title: Injection through untrusted input
description: Untrusted input reaching interpreters (SQL, OS commands, LDAP, templates) can alter the process's behaviour.
mitigation: Validate input against allow-lists, use parameterised queries and safe APIs, avoid dynamic code evaluation.

title: Cross-site scripting alters pages served to users
description: Unencoded user content rendered in pages lets attackers run script in other users' browsers.
mitigation: Context-aware output encoding, a strict Content-Security-Policy, framework auto-escaping.

title: Cross-site request forgery triggers unintended state changes
description: A malicious site causes the user's browser to send authenticated, state-changing requests.
mitigation: Anti-forgery tokens, SameSite cookies, require non-simple requests for state changes.

title: Compromised dependency or build pipeline
description: Malicious code introduced through a third-party package or the CI/CD pipeline runs with the process's privileges.
mitigation: Pin and verify dependencies, scan for known vulnerabilities, sign build artefacts, protect the pipeline.

title: Security-relevant events are not audited
description: Without an audit trail, misuse cannot be detected, investigated or attributed.
mitigation: Log authentication, authorisation failures and sensitive operations with user identity; ship logs to a central, append-only store.

title: Verbose errors reveal internal details
description: Stack traces, SQL errors or version banners help attackers map the system.
mitigation: Return generic error messages to callers, log details server-side only, remove version banners.

title: Insecure direct object reference exposes other users' data
description: Object identifiers supplied by the caller are used without checking that the caller owns the object.
mitigation: Enforce object-level authorisation on every access; prefer unguessable identifiers as defence in depth.

title: Secrets embedded in code or configuration
description: API keys, passwords or connection strings in source, images or config files can leak.
mitigation: Load secrets from a secret manager or managed identity at runtime; scan repositories for secrets.

title: Resource exhaustion through excessive requests
description: Floods of requests or expensive operations exhaust CPU, memory, threads or connections.
mitigation: Rate limiting, request size limits, timeouts, autoscaling and back-pressure.

title: Crafted input triggers expensive processing
description: Inputs such as deeply nested JSON, regex backtracking (ReDoS) or decompression bombs consume disproportionate resources.
mitigation: Bound input size and depth, use linear-time regex engines or timeouts, limit decompression ratios.

title: Missing function-level authorisation
description: Administrative or privileged functions are reachable by ordinary users because authorisation is checked only in the UI.
mitigation: Enforce role/permission checks server-side on every function; deny by default.

title: Compromise yields elevated privileges
description: The process runs with high privileges, so any code execution flaw gives an attacker those privileges.
mitigation: Run with least privilege, drop capabilities, sandbox or containerise, separate privileged functions into a small, hardened component.

title: Remote code execution through unsafe deserialisation or parsing
description: Deserialising untrusted data or parsing complex formats with vulnerable libraries can execute attacker code.
mitigation: Avoid polymorphic deserialisation of untrusted data, keep parsers patched, validate formats strictly.

title: Data modified by unauthorised parties
description: Weak access control on the store allows data to be altered directly, bypassing the application.
mitigation: Restrict write access to the owning service identity, use least-privilege database roles, enable change auditing.

title: Tampering goes undetected
description: Without integrity protection, modified records or files are indistinguishable from legitimate ones.
mitigation: Sign or MAC critical records, use checksums and versioning, monitor for unexpected changes.

title: Audit log can be altered or deleted
description: An attacker who can edit the log can erase evidence of their actions.
mitigation: Append-only / WORM storage, forward logs off-host, restrict delete permissions, hash-chain entries.

title: Sensitive data at rest is not encrypted
description: Disk theft, backups or snapshot access expose data stored in clear text.
mitigation: Encrypt at rest with managed keys, protect backups and snapshots with the same controls.

title: Stored credentials can be recovered
description: Passwords or secrets stored reversibly or with weak hashing can be recovered after a breach.
mitigation: Hash passwords with a slow, salted algorithm (Argon2id, bcrypt, PBKDF2); keep other secrets in a secret manager.

title: Over-broad read access to the store
description: Accounts, services or public endpoints can read more data than they need.
mitigation: Least-privilege read permissions, no public access, row/column-level security for sensitive data.

title: Store becomes unavailable or full
description: Storage exhaustion, lock contention or outage makes dependent processes fail.
mitigation: Quotas, monitoring and alerting on capacity, replication and tested backups.

title: Data in transit modified by a man-in-the-middle
description: Without integrity protection an attacker on the network path can alter requests or responses.
mitigation: Use TLS 1.2+ with certificate validation; consider message signing for high-value payloads.

title: Captured messages are replayed
description: Valid messages are captured and sent again to repeat an operation.
mitigation: Nonces or timestamps with short validity, idempotency keys, sequence numbers.

title: Data in transit is readable on the network
description: Unencrypted traffic can be captured and read by anyone on the network path.
mitigation: Encrypt the channel with TLS (or mTLS between services).

title: Sensitive data exposed over a public network
description: Traffic crossing the internet is exposed to interception and endpoint impersonation.
mitigation: TLS with strict certificate validation, HSTS for web traffic, minimise sensitive data in the payload.

title: More data than necessary crosses the trust boundary
description: Responses or messages leaving a trust zone contain fields the receiver does not need.
mitigation: Use explicit response DTOs, filter fields at the boundary, classify data and review what leaves each zone.

title: Channel is flooded or interrupted
description: Volumetric attacks or network failures interrupt communication along this flow.
mitigation: DDoS protection at the edge, timeouts and retries with back-off, circuit breakers, redundancy.

title: Oversized or malformed payloads disrupt the receiver
description: Very large or malformed messages consume resources or crash the receiving process.
mitigation: Enforce maximum message size, schema validation at the receiver, streaming limits.
